content: 1. Governments and employers must ensure that mental health is given equal importance to physical health in occupational health and safety (OSH) laws, policies, and practices. This includes revising existing frameworks to explicitly include mental health provisions and ensuring that mental disorders are recognized as occupational diseases in national lists, in alignment with the International Labour Organization (ILO) standards. 2. Occupational health definitions should always encompass both physical and mental health. Workplaces should adapt tasks to match workers' physical and mental capabilities or provide alternative employment without loss of pay or seniority when necessary. 3. Preventive measures should be prioritized over reactive measures, such as compensation. Employers should focus on assessing and managing psychosocial risks, including violence, harassment, and discrimination, while protecting the employment and income of workers affected by mental health conditions. 4. Workers and their representatives should actively participate in identifying psychosocial hazards and be consulted on actions to mitigate associated risks, just as they would for other workplace hazards. 5. Governments should build capacity for managing psychosocial risks within occupational health services and ensure compliance with legal frameworks through trained labor inspectors who can provide advice, investigate, and enforce regulations. 6. Employers should integrate mental health into their OSH management systems as a core component, not as an optional add-on. This integration should span all aspects of the management system, including policy, organization, planning, implementation, evaluation, and improvement. 7. Workplace mental health initiatives should emphasize collective measures based on thorough risk assessments and involve meaningful participation from workers and their representatives. Workers should be informed and trained about measures to prevent psychosocial risks. 8. Employers should manage workplace changes, such as restructuring or staffing adjustments, in ways that minimize psychosocial risks. Flexible working arrangements, participatory decision-making, and workload adjustments can help workers prioritize work-life balance. 9. Suicide prevention strategies in the workplace may include restricting access to means of suicide, such as pesticides or medications, and implementing organizational interventions to address psychosocial risk factors. 10. Organizational interventions that address psychosocial risks can reduce emotional distress and improve work-related outcomes, such as job satisfaction, absenteeism, and performance. These interventions should be universally implemented and tailored to specific workplace conditions. 11. Governments and employers should promote mental health at work by strengthening awareness, providing opportunities for early recognition of mental health conditions, and implementing evidence-based interventions. These include manager training, mental health literacy training for workers, and individual interventions. 12. Manager training should enhance knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to mental health, enabling managers to recognize when to direct employees to appropriate support services. This training should not aim to turn managers into mental health care providers but should empower them to advocate for workplace mental health initiatives. 13. Training for workers in mental health literacy and awareness can reduce stigma, improve understanding of mental health, and encourage help-seeking behaviors. Such training should be delivered by competent trainers, preferably during paid working hours, and involve individuals with lived experience of mental health conditions as co-facilitators. 14. Individual interventions, such as stress management training, relaxation techniques, and mindfulness, can help workers build skills to manage stress and reduce mental health symptoms. These interventions should be part of a broader program that includes preventive and supportive measures. 15. Employers should verify the quality and effectiveness of any mental health interventions by consulting experts. Digital self-help tools for stress management are popular but should be used alongside other comprehensive workplace mental health programs. 16. Workers with mental health conditions should have access to evidence-based psychological treatments, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, problem-solving therapy, or interpersonal therapy, preferably outside the workplace. 17. Governments and employers must uphold the right to work for individuals with mental health conditions through person-centered, recovery-oriented strategies. These strategies should support individuals in gaining, sustaining, and thriving in employment. 18. WHO guidelines recommend three evidence-based interventions to support workers with mental health conditions: reasonable accommodations at work, return-to-work programs, and supported employment initiatives.
